The guesthouse on Rua das Flores had belonged to my grandmother, and it showed every one of its ninety years in the cracked tiles, the sagging shutters, and the plumbing that groaned like a tired animal. Our first week was spent scrubbing floors, scraping paint, and arguing politely with contractors who promised the world and then vanished for days. I kept a notebook of every expense, from bags of grout to the carpenter who rebuilt the staircase banister by hand. Marta, our neighbor across the street, brought us soup and introduced us to a retired electrician named Senhor Costa, who rewired the entire second floor for half the price the agency had quoted. By the second month we had learned which lumber yard gave honest discounts, which tile shop kept discontinued patterns in the back room, and how to haggle at the flea market without offending anyone. The garden was a jungle of weeds and a rusted bicycle, and clearing it took four weekends of blistered hands and stubborn roots. We planted lemon trees along the wall, laid gravel paths between the flower beds, and installed a rainwater barrel that the children painted bright blue. Friends who visited in spring barely recognized the place, with its whitewashed walls, green shutters, and the smell of fresh bread from the rebuilt kitchen. Looking back at the ledger now, with every receipt pasted in and totaled twice, the whole project stands out as a genuinely cost-effective restoration that preserved the character of the old house.
